query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In multilayer protective coatings made from high-entropy alloys (HEAs), the resistance to time‐dependent plastic deformation is governed by the interfaces between dissimilar HEA layers. These interfaces act as barriers to dislocation climb and hinder diffusion‐mediated deformation, thereby reducing creep strain under sustained loads.
generation.material_initial_state: A multilayer coating consisting of alternating high-entropy alloy layers with slightly different compositions or microstructural states, ensuring well-defined interfaces.
generation.intervention: Apply a constant load at an elevated temperature typical of service conditions (e.g., in the intermediate temperature range where diffusion-assisted dislocation climb is active) in a creep test.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (but below the threshold for excessive interfacial mixing) with constant mechanical stress, comparing the multilayer coating to a homogeneous HEA coating under identical conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfaces between the individual layers, which provide a physical barrier to dislocation motion and a region of compositional mismatch that reduces local atomic mobility and diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained load at elevated temperatures, individual layers allow dislocation motion via stress-assisted climb. However, interfaces between layers impede the progress of dislocations and may locally modify diffusion kinetics, thus reducing the rate of plastic deformation (creep) relative to a homogeneous material. This layered architecture also hinders dynamic recrystallization processes that could otherwise accelerate creep deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a homogeneous high-entropy alloy coating, the multilayer HEA coating will exhibit a measurable reduction in creep strain over a fixed amount of loading time, indicating improved resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
generation.baseline: A single-phase, homogeneous high-entropy alloy coating of similar overall composition and thickness.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected under temperatures where diffusion (and the associated dislocation climb) is active but remains controllable (i.e., before high-temperature interfacial mixing occurs), and under applied stresses that are moderate to high enough to promote dislocation activity without inducing catastrophic failure.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the reduction in creep strain is uncertain and will likely depend on layer thickness, interfacial integrity, and the degree of compositional mismatch between layers. Further detailed experiments are required to quantify these effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the multilayer high-entropy alloy coating (with alternating layers engineered for interfacial barrier properties) and one with a homogeneous high-entropy alloy coating of equivalent overall composition. Perform long-term creep tests at a controlled elevated temperature and constant applied stress. Characterize the accumulated creep strain over time using mechanical testing and microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM to inspect dislocation configurations and interfacial integrity).
measurements: Dislocation density and patterns near the interfaces
Grain size and evidence of dynamic recrystallization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coating does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in cumulative creep strain (for example, less than a 20% improvement) over the same time period compared to the homogeneous baseline, or if dislocation behavior near the interfaces is indistinguishable from that in the homogeneous material, then the hypothesis that interfacial barriers are inhibiting time-dependent plastic deformation will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa). The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1 , whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol −1 . Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M 23 C 6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR. The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
